title: Harbor and Typewriter
premise: In the port city of Vellamare, on the eve of the Harbor Revolution, Astrid Reyes works in her late father's print shop, surviving by printing only what the Provisional Committee approves and forgetting everything else. When a six-year-old boy named Tomas is abandoned at her door with a note reading 'forget the face,' she recognizes the child of a purged archivist and realizes the Committee is erasing people as systematically as it prints its own history. Hiding Tomas, Astrid assembles a forbidden counter-record from her father's hidden type molds and the testimonies of the shop's found family—an old compositor, a smuggler, a disgraced censor. As the revolution turns on its own, she must print the true history and distribute it before the victors' historians seal the archive, choosing at last between safety and witness. The book ends with the record smuggled onto a departing ship and Astrid, publicly 'forgotten' herself, quietly opening a new print shop where Tomas's face is the first thing set in type.
about_author: Silas Ishikawa is the pen name of a former newspaper compositor who spent a decade in coastal archives restoring water-damaged periodicals. Harbor and Typewriter is his third novel, drawn from his obsession with the printers who outlasted the regimes that employed them.

chapters.title: The Weight of Silent Letters
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She sorts type in the Reyes print shop, navigating a Committee inspection with practiced silences while her apprentice Mira watches. Establishes the rules of survival under censorship. Emotional beat: the loneliness of a life built on omission, and Astrid's pride in the craft that keeps her invisible.

chapters.title: A Child at the Door
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, pre-dawn. A boy, Tomas, is left on the shop step with a note instructing her to forget his face. She recognizes the archivist Elena Voss's features in him. Emotional beat: fear warring with an old, buried instinct to protect; the first crack in seven years of careful silence.

chapters.title: The Committee's New History
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She is ordered to print an official account of the Harbor Uprising that contradicts what she saw with her own eyes. Her old compositor, Bram, quietly refuses to set one line. Emotional beat: the sickening recognition that the revolution she survived has become the thing she feared.

chapters.title: What Bram Remembers
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The old compositor recalls the purges of the previous regime and the night Astrid's father hid his own molds. He tells Astrid about the hidden cache. Emotional beat: grief passed down like an heirloom, and the first suggestion that forgetting is a choice, not a fate.

chapters.title: The Smuggler's Tide
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The harbor smuggler Odile Ferro, who runs contraband ink, agrees to move 'paper, not people'—until she sees Tomas. Emotional beat: gruff self-interest softening into complicity; the found family begins to assemble around the child.

chapters.title: Faces in the Molds
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. She and Tomas find her father's hidden type molds, including a complete second alphabet for printing forbidden texts. Tomas asks why his mother's face is 'on the list.' Emotional beat: wonder and dread entwined; the shop transforms from refuge to arsenal.

chapters.title: The Censor's Visit
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Censor Ivo Kastel, a former friend of her father, inspects the shop and lingers over Tomas's presence, saying nothing. Emotional beat: terror laced with ambiguity—Kastel is either a threat, an ally, or a man testing his own conscience.

chapters.title: Testimony of the Fishwives
chapters.summary: Mira's POV. Sent on an errand, Mira secretly collects accounts from fishwives who witnessed the harbor massacre the Committee denies. Emotional beat: the apprentice's coming-of-age, discovering that ordinary people have been waiting for someone to ask.

chapters.title: Ink and Ashes
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. A rival smuggler informs to the Committee; Odile burns her own ledgers to protect the network. Emotional beat: the cost of loyalty, and the dawning understanding that the record they're building is worth more than any cargo.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Wasn't There
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas explores the shop, learning letters, and overhears adults debating whether sending him away would keep everyone safe. Emotional beat: a child's quiet terror of being forgotten again, which hardens the adults' resolve.

chapters.title: Kastel's Bargain
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Kastel returns alone and reveals he kept his own forbidden archive for years, offering a page of it—if Astrid prints his testimony too. Emotional beat: wary alliance; the enemy censor becomes the record's most unlikely contributor.

chapters.title: The Historian's Deadline
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. The Committee announces the official Archive will be sealed at the Victory Festival in six weeks, after which all contrary accounts become sedition. Emotional beat: the clock starts; hope curdles into urgency as Astrid calculates the impossible scale of printing in secret.

chapters.title: Night Shift
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The found family prints through the nights—fishwives' testimony, Kastel's pages, the true harbor account—while Astrid sets type with her father's molds. Emotional beat: exhausted communion; the shop hums like a heartbeat, and Bram finally forgives himself for decades of silence.

chapters.title: Mira Is Followed
chapters.summary: Mira's POV. Collecting the last testimony, Mira realizes she's being watched and leads her tail away from the fishwives at real risk. Emotional beat: fear and fierce competence; the apprentice proves she is no longer a child to be shielded.

chapters.title: The Informer's Name
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. Odile traces the betrayal to the rival smuggler and faces a choice: hand him to the Committee and expose the route, or let him go and stay vulnerable. Emotional beat: moral corrosion of the revolution; power corrupts even those who only wanted to survive.

chapters.title: A Raid, Delayed
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Kastel warns of an imminent raid; the family hides Tomas and the molds minutes before soldiers tear the shop apart. Emotional beat: violation and relief in the same breath; Astrid understands the shop will never be safe again.

chapters.title: The Festival Approaches
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. With the Archive sealing in days, the group plans distribution: Odile's ship, Mira's fishwife network, Kastel's access to the Archive itself. Emotional beat: terrified resolve; each member confesses what they stand to lose, binding them irrevocably.

chapters.title: What the Censor Kept
chapters.summary: Kastel's POV. Kastel enters the sealed Archive under festival pretenses and plants the counter-record inside the official vault, knowing he will likely be caught. Emotional beat: redemption purchased at the price of everything; a man finally on the right side of history, too late for himself.

chapters.title: The Night of the Festival
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, climax. Fireworks cover the loading of three thousand pamphlets onto Odile's ship; soldiers close in; Bram is arrested as a decoy and Astrid must choose between saving him and saving the record. Emotional beat: the climax's brutal arithmetic—witness versus love, and no clean choice.

chapters.title: The Ship That Carried Paper
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The ship slips the harbor with the record aboard as the city burns behind it; Odile learns Bram's fate and Astrid's sacrifice of her own name to the Committee's 'forgotten' list. Emotional beat: triumph shadowed by loss; the truth is free but its keepers are not.

chapters.title: Forgotten on Purpose
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV. Declared erased, Astrid and Tomas slip out of Vellamare with Mira, passing her father's old shop one last time. Emotional beat: mourning and strange liberation; invisibility, once a cage, is now her own chosen instrument.

chapters.title: The First Line
chapters.summary: Astrid's POV, epilogue. In a smaller harbor town, a new print shop opens; Astrid sets the first page of a free press, and its opening line is Tomas's name in full, his face described so no one can be told to forget it. Emotional beat: quiet, earned hope—memory set in type, and a family that chose itself.
